overview: National Australia Bank (NAB) is one of Australia's big four banks, providing retail, business, corporate and institutional banking and financial services to around 10 million customers across Australia and New Zealand, with smaller operations in Asia, the UK, Europe and the US. NAB traces its franchise strength to business and agribusiness banking, where it holds market leadership, and operates Bank of New Zealand (BNZ) as its wholly owned NZ subsidiary alongside the digital-only ubank brand. The Group had total assets of A$1.11 trillion, gross loans and acceptances of A$781.5bn and total customer deposits of A$658.4bn as at 30 September 2025 (FY ends 30 September).

business_model.summary: NAB earns the large majority of revenue from net interest income (lending margin on loans funded by deposits and wholesale funding) supplemented by fee, trading and markets income. Its four reporting divisions are Business and Private Banking (B&PB, its most profitable and highest-share segment), Personal Banking (mortgages, cards, deposits), Corporate and Institutional Banking (C&IB, institutional/markets/transactional banking) and New Zealand Banking (BNZ). Revenue is largely recurring (net interest margin on a large, sticky loan/deposit book) rather than transactional, though markets and treasury income is more volatile quarter to quarter.
business_model.customer_type: Mixed: retail/consumer (Personal Banking, ubank), SME/business (B&PB - one in four Australian SMEs, one in three agribusinesses), and large corporate/institutional (C&IB); BNZ serves 1.4m+ NZ personal, SME, agri and private banking customers
business_model.geographic_mix: Predominantly Australia and New Zealand; smaller offices in the US, UK, Europe and Asia supporting C&IB. FY2025 net profit split approximately: Business & Private Banking largest contributor, Personal Banking, Corporate & Institutional Banking and New Zealand Banking (BNZ) each material; NZ Banking net profit declined 3.0% YoY in FY2025 amid weaker NZ economic conditions

main_competitors: ING Australia, digital neobanks and non-bank/private credit lenders
competitive_position.market_position: Australia's leading business bank by market share (one in four SME customers, one in three agribusiness customers), and NAB is a Domestic Systemically Important Bank (D-SIB); ranked among the big four that collectively dominate Australian banking. BNZ is New Zealand's largest business bank and one of its fastest-growing retail banks.

moat_factors.description: Deep, decades-long SME and agribusiness relationships with high switching costs (transaction banking, cash management, lending covenants) underpin NAB's largest and most profitable division

moat_factors.factor: Scale and regulatory barriers to entry
moat_factors.description: D-SIB status, APRA capital/licensing requirements and network scale create high barriers for new entrants; NAB is one of only four Australian majors
Large, granular deposit base (A$658bn) funds lending more cheaply than wholesale-funded non-bank competitors, though intensifying deposit competition is eroding this edge
Long-standing brand recognition, though reputational damage from AUSTRAC and payroll remediation issues has weighed on trust metrics

Ongoing technology modernisation and a change in software capitalisation policy (raising the capitalisation threshold from $5m to $20m) suggest a legacy cost base and less mature technology stack versus digital-first competitors

weaknesses: Personal Banking (mortgages) is the most commoditised, price-competitive segment and has lagged retail-oriented peers on growth
History of conduct, compliance and payroll remediation failures (AUSTRAC Enforceable Undertaking, ongoing payroll review) creates recurring cost and reputational drag
Elevated digital/technology outage frequency versus big-four peers (NAB had ~831 minutes of downtime in the 12 months prior to a further major September 2026 outage)
Heavy exposure to cyclical Australian/NZ mortgage and CRE lending concentrates credit risk in two closely correlated housing markets
Weaker recent EPS growth and PE re-rating versus peers, per external analyst commentary

growth_drivers: Three-priority strategy (announced November 2024): growing business banking, driving deposit growth and strengthening proprietary home lending — business lending +9.3% and deposits +7.4% in FY2025
Proprietary mortgage distribution mix improving materially (41% of FY2025 drawdowns via NAB bankers, rising to 47.7% in 1H26) to reduce broker-channel margin compression
Business and Private Banking momentum continuing into 1H26 (+5.4% growth) as the highest-returning division
New Zealand Banking (BNZ) gaining share in household deposits and lending despite a soft NZ economy
Digital/AI investment (fraud detection, agentic AI, faster lending decisioning) targeted to cut cost-to-serve and speed up loan approvals (~20% faster 'yes' decisions in B&PB)
ubank digital bank scaling rapidly (1.05m+ customers, +24% YoY) as a lower-cost acquisition channel for younger customers
Housing affordability financing ambition expanded to $60bn by 2030 (from $6bn goal achieved four years early), and $80bn cumulative environmental finance ambition by 2030, opening new lending pools
Ongoing capital return via buybacks ($8bn completed since August 2021) and neutralisation of the dividend reinvestment plan, supporting per-share metrics despite modest earnings growth
Productivity program targeting >$450m of cost benefits in FY2026 to offset inflation in technology and compliance spend

business.description: Broker-driven price competition in Australian mortgages and rising deposit competition are compressing margins and threatening market share, especially in Personal Banking

business.risk: Concentration in Australian/NZ housing and agribusiness
business.description: Residential and commercial real estate loans are a material share of the loan book; a large agribusiness lending book is exposed to commodity price, weather and China-trade shocks
Repeated digital banking outages (including a major multi-service outage on 23 September 2026) highlight technology fragility versus peers and payments-infrastructure criticality
Private credit funds, digital platforms and large technology companies are competing for lending and payments relationships with lower cost bases and lighter regulation

financial.description: NIM has been broadly stable (1.74% FY2025, 1.81% 1H26) but remains sensitive to deposit mix, wholesale funding costs and lending competition

1H26 credit impairment charge rose to $706m from $485m in 2H25, with forward-looking provisions up $300m amid fuel-cost/geopolitical and sector-specific stress (agriculture, transport, construction, commercial property)
Significant reliance on offshore wholesale funding markets; a ratings downgrade would raise funding costs and could tighten liquidity

financial.risk: Earnings volatility from accounting policy changes
financial.description: 1H26 cash earnings were reduced by $949m due to a change in software capitalisation policy (threshold raised from $5m to $20m), illustrating how non-cash/accounting items can distort period comparisons

regulatory.description: A further 1.5% of RWA Loss-Absorbing Capacity requirement applies from 1 January 2026; AT1 capital reform takes effect from 1 January 2027; RBNZ is separately reviewing BNZ's capital settings

NAB's AUSTRAC Enforceable Undertaking was cancelled in July 2025, but a broader payroll-related benefits review remains ongoing with the Fair Work Ombudsman; FY2025 flagged an incremental ~$130m payroll remediation hit on top of ~$250m historically, with total costs still uncertain

regulatory.risk: AML/CTF and financial crime regime reform
regulatory.description: Legislative reform to Australia's AML/CTF regime and a new Scams Prevention Framework require substantial compliance investment with guidance still being finalised
NZ Commerce Commission and government reviews into banking competition, plus the Customer and Product Data Act 2025, are likely to raise compliance costs and competitive pressure for BNZ

macro.description: Bank earnings and credit quality are closely tied to house prices, interest rates and unemployment in two markets that have diverged (Australia resilient, NZ contracting through much of 2025)
RBA cut the cash rate from 4.35% to 3.60% between Feb-Aug 2025 with further cuts possible; RBNZ cut the OCR from 5.50% to 2.50% by October 2025 — further easing affects NIM and loan demand
Australia and NZ export income is materially exposed to Chinese demand and global tariff/trade tensions; Middle East conflict has already prompted higher fuel-related provisioning

macro.risk: Global market volatility and tariff policy
macro.description: US tariff policy uncertainty and broader geopolitical instability are flagged by management as key drivers of a 'more volatile macro environment' entering FY2026

macro_factors.industry_outlook: Australian system credit growth strengthened to 7.3% YoY to September 2025 (from 5.8%), supported by resilient GDP growth (~1.8%), falling inflation and RBA rate cuts; NZ system credit growth remains modest (4.3%) amid a weaker NZ economy (GDP down ~1.6% from its March 2024 peak) though a recovery is expected as RBNZ easing and high commodity prices flow through
macro_factors.cyclicality: Moderate-to-high — bank earnings, credit losses and loan growth are tied to the Australian/NZ economic and housing cycle; NAB's heavy agribusiness and business lending exposure adds additional commodity-cycle sensitivity
macro_factors.interest_rate_sensitivity: High — net interest margin, loan demand and deposit costs are directly affected by RBA/RBNZ policy rates and the shape of the yield curve; a stabilising-to-easing rate environment in FY2026 is broadly supportive of loan growth but pressures deposit margins
key_input_costs: Wholesale/offshore funding costs and credit spreads
Regulatory capital costs (Tier 2/AT1 issuance under LAC reform)

recent_developments.event: Major multi-service digital outage (mobile app, internet banking, NAB Connect, Trade, Broker, JBWere and phone lines) affecting customers for several hours; most services restored same day, cause undisclosed

Goldman Sachs upgraded NAB from 'Strong Sell' to 'Hold', having initiated coverage with a Sell rating (AUD 38 price target) in October 2025 citing weak Personal Banking metrics and competitive pressure on B&PB

1H FY2026 results: statutory net profit A$2.75bn, down 19.3% YoY, driven by a $949m cash-earnings hit from a change in software capitalisation policy (threshold raised from $5m to $20m, accelerating $1,347m of amortisation); underlying cash earnings ex-notable items up 2.3% half-on-half; interim dividend held at 85 cents fully franked; ~$1.8bn raised via a partially-underwritten DRP to lift pro forma CET1 to 12.05%

Credit impairment charge rose to $706m in 1H26 from $485m in 2H25, including $300m of additional forward-looking provisions tied to fuel-supply/cost stress in Agriculture, Transport & Storage, Manufacturing, Construction and Commercial Property sectors amid Middle East conflict-related volatility

FY2025 full-year results: cash ROE 11.4%, statutory net profit A$6.76bn (down 2.9% YoY), CET1 ratio 11.70%, dividend 170 cents per share (up from 169 cents), $8bn cumulative buybacks completed since August 2021
Completed sale of remaining 20% stake in MLC Life to Nippon Life for A$497m, exiting life insurance entirely
AUSTRAC confirmed cancellation of NAB's Enforceable Undertaking (entered April 2022) following completion of an independent auditor's review; NAB continues implementing residual recommendations

NAB flagged an additional ~$130m FY2025 opex hit from a broadened payroll remediation review into current and historical enterprise agreements, on top of ~$250m of prior remediation; review remains ongoing with the Fair Work Ombudsman

Multiple Executive Leadership Team changes: Andrew Auerbach (B&PB, June 2025), Pete Steel (Digital, Data & AI, Nov 2025), Shane Conway (Transformation, Dec 2025) and Inder Singh (Group CFO & Strategy, expected March 2026) — significant management transition underway

items.notes: Cost growth ex large notable items, reflecting continued technology/personnel investment offset by productivity gains
Targeted cost-out program to fund technology and compliance investment while limiting overall expense growth
~$1.8bn raised via a partially-underwritten dividend reinvestment plan with 1.5% discount following the software capitalisation policy change, to bolster capital in a volatile macro environment

items.target: target payout ratio maintained (interim FY2026 dividend held at 85 cents, fully franked)
items.notes: Board reiterated capital return discipline; final FY2025 dividend was 85 cents, full-year 170 cents

items.target: continued growth in business banking, deposits and proprietary home lending share
items.notes: Proprietary mortgage drawdown share rose from 41.4% (2H25) to 47.7% (1H26); management targets continued gains in all three strategic priority areas

guidance.management_commentary: CEO Andrew Irvine described 1H26 as reflecting 'continued disciplined execution' with underlying profit up 6.4% half-on-half ex notable items, but flagged that 'geopolitical tensions have created a more volatile macro economic environment' and that the bank had taken pre-emptive action (higher forward-looking provisions, capital raising via DRP) to 'bolster our balance sheet' heading into a period of increased uncertainty. Management reiterated the three-priority strategy (business banking, deposits, proprietary home lending) as the primary driver of returns.

bull_case: Market-leading, high-margin business and agribusiness banking franchise (B&PB) is NAB's biggest profit driver and continues to outgrow the rest of the group (+5.4% in 1H26)
Improving proprietary mortgage distribution mix (47.7% of drawdowns in 1H26, up from 41.4%) should reduce broker-channel margin drag over time
Strong capital position (CET1 ~11.6-12.05% pro forma) and continued capital return (buybacks plus fully franked dividends) support shareholder returns even with modest earnings growth
AUSTRAC Enforceable Undertaking cancellation (July 2025) removes a multi-year regulatory overhang, and management is investing in AI/technology to lower cost-to-serve and speed decisioning
BNZ provides diversified NZ exposure with market share gains in a market poised to recover as RBNZ rate cuts and strong commodity export prices flow through
bear_case: Personal Banking (mortgages) faces structural margin compression from broker-driven price competition, and Goldman Sachs has flagged it as lacking a credible profit-growth catalyst
Recurring conduct/compliance failures (AUSTRAC, ongoing payroll remediation with uncertain total cost, Fair Work Ombudsman engagement) signal persistent execution and culture risk
Technology fragility — repeated digital outages, including a major September 2026 multi-service outage — raises operational risk and reputational concerns versus peers with better uptime records
1H26 results show rising credit impairment charges and higher forward-looking provisions, an early signal of a turning credit cycle amid geopolitical and cost-of-living pressures

Consensus analyst view is broadly Neutral-to-cautious (average target ~10% below recent price per some estimates), reflecting NAB's underperformance versus retail-oriented big-four peers on earnings growth and PE re-rating
